title: The Satipatthana, alone
tomorrow: should you steer your breath, or only watch it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sumedha cut her hair and kept talking until her family heard her: she chose. That closed the sisters. Now the Pali suttas, read alone, starting with a riddle.

A song can have twelve verses and one chorus, and the chorus is what you're humming at the bus stop. Read MN 10 straight through with nobody explaining it, and you hit something that looks like a copying mistake. Breathing. Then walking, standing, sitting, lying down. The parts of the body. Feelings. The mind. And after every single section, the same block of lines, word for word, again and again. Why would a sutta repeat itself like that?
screen: `TWELVE VERSES, ONE CHORUS.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE A COPYING MISTAKE.` → `THE SAME LINES, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the answer: the repeated lines aren't filler. They're the practice. The sections change what you look at; the refrain tells you how to look. In paraphrase: you stay with the body as body, inside and outside. You see it arising, and you see it passing. Mindfulness is simply there, just enough to know and keep knowing. And you rest, not leaning on anything, not grabbing at anything in the world. Then the next section starts, and the refrain comes back for feelings, for the mind, for the teachings themselves. Same how, new what. That's why reading alone matters. With a guide, the refrain is easy to skip. Alone, it keeps landing until you notice it's the point. The sutta opens by calling these four, body, feelings, mind and the teachings, ekayano maggo. English has put that more than one way: a path that goes one way, a direct path. Whichever word you choose, it means no detour. You don't have to get somewhere else first. Whatever is here is already the object.
screen: `THE REFRAIN IS THE PRACTICE.` · `ARISING, PASSING, NOT GRABBING.` · `SAME HOW, NEW WHAT.` · `EKAYANO MAGGO: NO DETOUR.` · then, large: `THE DIRECT PATH.`

segments.voice: Try the section on feelings. Each time something registers, a sound, an ache, a thought, notice only its tone: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. Then watch that tone arise and pass, without leaning toward it or away.
The Satipatthana: the sutta on the establishing of mindfulness, MN 10, four places to stand and one refrain for how to look.
The direct path: no detour, and what's here is enough to start. Sutta one, read alone.

howItsDone: The Satipatthana Sutta is a foundation for mindfulness practice in Theravada communities; some teachers have students work through one section at a time, returning to the refrain for each.

myth: the repeated lines in MN 10 are a copying mistake
they're the practice itself: the same way of looking, applied to each new object.
MN 10 covers body, feelings, mind and the teachings
four places to establish mindfulness, each with the same refrain.
mindfulness in MN 10 means emptying the mind of thoughts
the mind itself is one of the things you watch, arising and passing.

fork.setup: you're dreading a hard conversation tonight and can't focus on homework. what does MN 10 point you to?
options: make the dread itself the object: feel it, see it rise and pass
push the dread away first, then start the real practice
wait until the conversation is over to try again
fork.reveal: the direct path means no detour: feelings and the mind are already objects in the sutta. whatever is here is where it starts.

original.note: Pali: the establishing of mindfulness (sati). MN 10 is named for it.

trapdoor: what you thought: mindfulness is a relaxation trick.
what it means: four places to stand, body, feelings, mind and the teachings, and one refrain: see it arise, see it pass, lean on nothing.
what a scholar hears: MN 10, with a longer twin at DN 22; ekayano maggo has been rendered 'the only way', 'the direct path' and 'the one-way path'.
guess: the sutta on establishing mindfulness in four places
a set of breathing drills for falling asleep faster
the rules for how monks walk, stand and sit

chat.says: mom still hasn't said anything about art. i keep replaying it while i draw and my lines are garbage.
options: let the replay be the thing you watch: feel it rise and pass, then back to the hand.
stop drawing until mom answers. you can't focus till the whole thing is settled.
shove the feeling down and draw harder. feelings are just distractions from the work.
chat.meaning: MN 10's direct path has no detour: feelings and the mind are already objects. Watch them arise and pass, without grabbing.

tie.story: MN 10 repeats one refrain for body, feelings and mind: see it arise, see it pass, lean on nothing.
tie.friend: Mai can watch the worry about Mom come and go, then come back to her pencil.
tie.you: what keeps replaying for you, and could you watch it for a minute?

MN 10.meaning: the Satipatthana Sutta, tenth in the Middle-Length Discourses

ekayano maggo.meaning: Pali: a path going one way; a direct path

sutta.meaning: a discourse of the Buddha, in Pali

notes: The refrain paraphrased: contemplating the body as body internally, externally, both; the nature of arising, of passing away, of both; mindfulness 'there is a body' established just enough for knowledge and mindfulness; dwelling independent, not clinging to anything in the world. Confirm.

The hook lists sections loosely (breathing, postures, parts of the body, feelings, mind); the body section also has clear comprehension, elements and the charnel-ground contemplations, left out. The refrain also follows the dhammas section. Confirm the hook's 'after every single section' is accurate for the body subsections.
Ekayano maggo: the script says English has put it more than one way, without naming translators; the trapdoor names the three common renderings. Confirm.
'A song can have twelve verses' in the hook is an illustration, not a claim about the sutta.
